_readme: U1 — Building a sentence. The floor of the whole module and the first screen a beginner sees.
Ten points, all A1, no choice points (R1 §2 marks U1 as F/A only), so no `contrast` block is authored.
sequence_index values are drawn from this block's private band 1000-1099 and are ORDERED, not final.
The post-merge renumbering pass re-seats them topologically into the final 1..154.
Every grammatical label is defined in plain words at the point that introduces it. The reader is
assumed to know no grammar vocabulary at all: not 'noun', not 'verb', not 'subject'.

points.title: Putting a sentence together so that it says who does what

point_json.grammar_name: The English clause: subject, verb, object

teach.can_do: I can put a sentence together so that it says who is involved and what happens.
teach.why_it_matters: Everything taught later is this shape with something added to it. Get it wrong and a reader cannot read your sentence, only guess at it.
teach.meaning: An English sentence is built round two things and it falls over without either. First, the person or thing the sentence is about — call it the doer. Second, one word saying what the doer does, or what the doer is — call it the action word. The doer comes first and the action word comes straight after it. If the action lands on something, that thing comes third. Doer, action, thing acted on: that order almost never moves, and the order is what tells your reader who did what to whom.

form.pattern: doer + action word (+ the thing the action lands on)
notes: The doer comes first. English will not let you start with the action and add the doer later.
The thing the action lands on sits straight after the action word, with nothing pushed in between.
Every sentence needs its own action word, however short the sentence is.
form.negative: The word not goes with the action word and never in front of the doer: the coast path is not open.
form.question: Ask who or what is this about, then ask what do they do. If either answer is missing, the sentence is not finished.

left.role: who or what the sentence is about

right.role: what it does, and what that lands on
right.text: leaves the old market at eleven

spec.caption: Two boxes, always in this order. No English sentence gets to skip the first one.

worked_example.sentence: The council closed the footbridge at Sandmouth.
worked_example.why_this_form: The council is who the sentence is about, closed says what they did, and the footbridge is what the closing landed on. Three parts, in the only order English accepts.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Turn it round to the footbridge closed the council and every word is still real, but you have handed the bridge the job of shutting down a council.

notice_set.sentence: The new ferry carries eighty passengers.
notice_set.question: What is this sentence giving you news about?
notice_set.why: The sentence opens with the ferry, and everything after it is news about the ferry.

notice_set.sentence: The storm damaged the harbour wall.
notice_set.question: Which one took the damage?
notice_set.why: Whatever comes after the action word is what the action reached, and here it reached the wall.

notice_set.sentence: The harbour wall damaged the storm.
notice_set.question: Could this really happen?
notice_set.why: Every word is fine. The order has simply given the wall the job of wrecking a storm.

notice_set.sentence: Rain all week in the Verdon valley.
notice_set.question: Does this say what the rain did?
notice_set.why: There is nothing here saying what happened, so this is a heap of words rather than a piece of news.

notice_set.sentence: Halim repairs bicycles in a shed behind the station.
notice_set.question: What does Halim do?
notice_set.why: The word straight after Halim says what he does, and the words after that say what he does it to.

teach.rule_line: Name who it is about, then say what they do. Anything less is not yet a sentence.
teach.false_rule: That a long string of words counts as a sentence because it is long. Length proves nothing. Four words with someone doing something beat fifteen without.

errors.wrong: The long queue outside the ticket office every morning.
errors.right: A long queue forms outside the ticket office every morning.
errors.why_it_happens: The words paint a complete picture, so nothing feels missing to the writer. Nothing is missing except the one word saying what actually happens.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: forms.

errors.wrong: The depot opens at six the drivers arrive at half past five.
errors.right: The depot opens at six. The drivers arrive at half past five.
errors.why_it_happens: Two pieces of news arrive in one breath, so they get written in one breath. Speech puts a small pause here that writing has to spell out.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one full stop after six.

errors.wrong: The two engineers checks the pump every Friday.
errors.right: The two engineers check the pump every Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: An s has attached itself to whatever felt singular at the moment of writing. The action word has to look back at who it belongs to, and here that is two people.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on checks.

errors.wrong: The council the footbridge closed in October.
errors.right: The council closed the footbridge in October.
errors.why_it_happens: Many languages let the thing acted on come before the action, so the order sounds acceptable in the writer's head. English readers have to stop and work out who did what.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: closed goes in front of the footbridge.
errors.l1_note: Common for speakers of Japanese, Korean, Turkish and Hindi-Urdu.

pays_in.note: Every answer in the opening minutes is this shape, said quickly.
pays_in.model: I live in a small flat near the market and I walk to work.

pays_in.note: Every essay sentence rests on it, however long the sentence grows.
pays_in.model: Better street lighting reduces the number of accidents after dark.

pays_in.note: Finding who does what is how you answer a question about a long sentence.
pays_in.model: The survey team recorded the damage before the second storm arrived.

used_in.quote: Every answer on this card is a short run of these: something is named, and then something is said about it.

payload.sentence: The last bus from Marlow leaves at ten past eleven.
payload.question: What does this tell you about the last bus?

feedback.why_key: The words straight after the bus say what it does, and that is the whole of the news here.
feedback.feed_forward: Find who or what the sentence is about, then read straight on.

payload.sentence: The rain flooded the car park behind the clinic.
payload.question: What went under water?

feedback.why_key: Whatever sits after the action word is what the action reached, and the water reached the car park.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the words after the action to see what it landed on.

items.decision_cue: A long queue outside the new clinic every morning

payload.context: From a first draft of a letter to the council.
payload.sentence: A long queue outside the new clinic every morning.
reasons: nothing here says what the queue actually does
the queue has been put in the wrong place
there should be a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: You can picture it, which is why it slips through. Nothing in it says what happens.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that every sentence has a word saying what happens.

payload.context: From a note about the Ashfield line.
payload.stem: The morning trains ___ (leave) Ashfield before six.

expected: leave

feedback.why_key: Without this word the sentence names some trains and then stops, telling the reader nothing about them.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the word that says what happens before you stop.

payload.context: Two drivers talking at the depot gate.
payload.stem: The night shifts ___ (finish) before the first buses run.

expected: finish

feedback.why_key: Say the words without it and you have named the shifts without saying a single thing about them.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the sentence aloud and listen for the missing action.

payload.context: Build one sentence about the fieldwork on the Verdon.

expected: the survey team measured the water level every morning
every morning the survey team measured the water level

feedback.why_key: The team does the measuring and the water level is what gets measured. Swap them and the water starts doing the work.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the doer first and keep the action next to it.

payload.given: A queue at the ticket machine every morning.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that it says what the queue does.

expected: forms at the ticket machine every morning
builds up at the ticket machine every morning
grows at the ticket machine every morning

feedback.why_key: One word turns a picture into a piece of news, because now something is happening in it.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the word that says what happens, then read it back.

payload.audio_text: My brother mends bikes in a shed behind the flats.

expected: my brother mends bikes in a shed behind the flats

feedback.why_key: In quick speech the word doing the work is short and unstressed, and it is the first thing a listener drops.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the word straight after the person named.

payload.sentence: The market moved to the square in June the old site is still empty.

expected: in june. the old site
in June. The old site

feedback.why_key: Two pieces of news are sharing one breath. The full stop is the wall telling the reader where the first one ends.
feedback.feed_forward: Put a full stop where the first piece of news ends.

items.decision_cue: The two reporters covers the harbour story

payload.context: From a first draft about local news.
payload.sentence: The two reporters covers the harbour story every week.
reasons: the word for what they do does not match two people
the story has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two people are doing it, so the word for what they do has to be the one that goes with more than one.
feedback.feed_forward: Look back at who is doing it before you write the action.

payload.context: Two lines taken from different reports on the same night.
sentences: The lorry hit the barrier.
The barrier hit the lorry.
meanings: The barrier is the thing that took the blow.
The lorry is the thing that took the blow.

feedback.why_key: Nothing changed but which one came first, and that alone decided which one got damaged.
feedback.feed_forward: Read which thing comes first before you decide who did what.

payload.prompt_text: A block of flats near you has lost its lift. Write one sentence saying what that does to the people living on the top floor.

feedback.why_key: A complaint becomes an argument only when a sentence names who is affected and then says what happens to them.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the people first, then say what happens to them.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 1 card about your home town. Speak for forty seconds. Every sentence must name someone or something and then say what it does. Record it and listen for any sentence that stops early.

feedback.why_key: Under time pressure the word saying what happens is the first one to go missing, and a listener notices at once.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish each sentence before you start the next one.

points.title: Saying what someone or something is, with am, is and are

point_json.grammar_name: The present of be: am, is, are

teach.can_do: I can say what someone or something is, and what it is like, right now.
teach.why_it_matters: This is what English uses when nothing is happening and you are only saying what is so. Leave it out and the sentence has no engine.
teach.meaning: Some sentences report an event. Others report how things stand: who somebody is, where a thing is, what it is like. English refuses to say those with an empty middle. It puts in one small word — am, is or are — and that word carries the whole sentence. Which of the three you use is decided entirely by who or what stands in front of it, and never by what follows it.

form.pattern: I am · he, she, it or one thing is · you, we, they or more than one thing are
notes: Choose it by looking left, at who or what the sentence is about, never right.
In speech and in a message the three shrink: I'm, she's, they're, it's. In an essay, write them out.
One thing takes is and more than one takes are, however many words sit in between.
form.negative: Put not straight after it: I am not, she is not, they are not. Out loud, isn't and aren't.
form.question: Move it in front of the doer: Are you ready? Is the office open?

rungs.text: The office is not open on Sunday.
The figures are set out below.

worked_example.sentence: The two lifts in the north block are out of order again.
worked_example.why_this_form: Nothing happens in this sentence. It only reports how things stand, and are is the word that carries it. Two lifts pull are rather than is.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Write is instead and the sentence quietly claims there is one lift, which fights with the two you named a moment earlier.

notice_set.sentence: My cousins are at the technical college on Norland Road.
notice_set.question: How many cousins is this about?
notice_set.why: are is the word English uses when more than one thing stands in front of it.

notice_set.sentence: The flat above the bakery is empty.
notice_set.question: How many homes is this about?
notice_set.why: is goes with a single thing, and the single thing here is the flat rather than the bakery.

notice_set.sentence: I'm the one who locks up on Fridays.
notice_set.question: Who locks up?
notice_set.why: I'm is I am squeezed into one word, so the speaker is talking about themselves.

notice_set.sentence: The keys to the side gate are in the top drawer.
notice_set.question: Where would you look for the keys?
notice_set.why: are points back to the keys, so the rest of the sentence is telling you where they sit.

notice_set.sentence: Elif is not at the depot on Mondays.
notice_set.question: Could you find Elif at the depot on a Monday?
notice_set.why: not sits straight after is and turns the whole report the other way round.

teach.rule_line: Look left. One thing takes is, more than one takes are, and I takes am.
teach.false_rule: That is and are are noise you can drop because the meaning survives without them. The meaning does survive. English still refuses the gap.

errors.wrong: The waiting room very cold in the mornings.
errors.right: The waiting room is very cold in the mornings.
errors.why_it_happens: Many languages join a thing to its description with nothing in between, so the sentence sounds finished to the writer because the meaning has already arrived.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: is.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Russian, Arabic and Turkish.

errors.wrong: The prices at the station café is higher than in town.
errors.right: The prices at the station café are higher than in town.
errors.why_it_happens: The nearest thing to the gap is a single café, so the word gets chosen by whatever was said last rather than by what the sentence is about.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: is becomes are.

errors.wrong: The list of approved suppliers are on the noticeboard.
errors.right: The list of approved suppliers is on the noticeboard.
errors.why_it_happens: Suppliers sits right beside the gap, and by the time the sentence reaches the middle the single list has slipped out of mind.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: are becomes is.

errors.wrong: I am not sure where the office is, but I am happy to look.
errors.right: I'm not sure where the office is, but I'm happy to look.
errors.why_it_happens: Books print the full forms, so learners produce them everywhere. Out loud the full form lands as emphasis, and a whole answer of it sounds like an argument.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: I am becomes I'm.

pays_in.note: Introducing yourself, your home and your job runs almost entirely on this word.
pays_in.model: I'm from a small town on the coast and my family is still there.

pays_in.note: A letter describing a problem is built on it, sentence after sentence.
pays_in.model: The heating in the flat is unreliable and the windows are draughty.

pays_in.note: Speakers squeeze it down to almost nothing, and you must hear it to follow.
pays_in.model: She's on the late shift and they're both off tomorrow.

used_in.quote: Describing a home means saying what rooms are like, which is this word again and again.

payload.sentence: My brothers are out at work by seven.
payload.question: How many brothers is the speaker talking about?

feedback.why_key: are is the word that goes with more than one, so the number is settled before you reach the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the small word in the middle to count the people.

payload.sentence: The window in the two upstairs rooms is painted shut.
payload.question: How many windows is this about?

feedback.why_key: is looks back to the single window, not to the two rooms sitting beside it.
feedback.feed_forward: Track the small word back to the thing it belongs to.

payload.context: From a note to a landlord about repairs.
payload.sentence: The kitchen tap still loose after the visit last week.
reasons: nothing carries the sentence between the tap and its description
the tap has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The description arrives and the meaning lands, but English will not join the two halves across an empty middle.
feedback.feed_forward: Put is or are between the thing and its description.

payload.context: From a message to a course tutor.
payload.stem: The two rooms on the ground floor ___ free after four.

expected: are

feedback.why_key: Two rooms stand in front of the gap, and more than one thing always pulls are.
feedback.feed_forward: Count what stands in front of the gap before you fill it.

payload.context: A tenant on the phone about the block she lives in.
payload.stem: The lift ___ (not be) working again this week.

expected: is not
isn't
isnt

feedback.why_key: not sits straight after the word carrying the sentence, and out loud the two squeeze into one.
feedback.feed_forward: Put not straight after is, are or am.

payload.context: Build one sentence for a notice on the door.

expected: the staff room is not open before eight

feedback.why_key: The word carrying the sentence comes straight after the room, and not comes straight after that.
feedback.feed_forward: Place is, then not, then the description.

payload.given: The hallway. Very dark since the bulb went.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence saying what the hallway is like.

expected: is very dark since the bulb went
is very dark because the bulb has gone
is very dark now that the bulb has gone

feedback.why_key: One word welds the description onto the hallway, and the two half-sentences become one piece of news.
feedback.feed_forward: Join the thing to its description with is or are.

payload.audio_text: They're both at the college and she's on the late bus.

expected: they're both at the college and she's on the late bus
they are both at the college and she is on the late bus
theyre both at the college and shes on the late bus

feedback.why_key: Squeezed down to a single sound, this word is easy to miss, and missing it costs you the whole shape of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small sound riding on the end of the person.

payload.sentence: The cost of the two new ferries are higher than the council expected.
payload.error_span: of the two new ferries are

expected: of the two new ferries is

feedback.why_key: The sentence is about one cost. Two ferries sit next to the gap and pull the wrong word out of the writer.
feedback.feed_forward: Look past the words in between to the thing the sentence is about.

payload.context: A candidate answering the first question at an interview.
payload.sentence: I'm on the late shift most weeks, so I'm free in the mornings.
reasons: the squeezed forms do not belong in speech
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
the word in the middle does not match the speaker
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Squeezing them is what speakers actually do. Writing them out in full here would sound like a correction rather than an answer.
feedback.feed_forward: Squeeze am, is and are whenever you are speaking.

payload.context: Two lines from a housing report on the same street.
sentences: The flat above the surgery is empty.
The flats above the surgery are empty.
meanings: One home is standing unused.
Several homes are standing unused.

feedback.why_key: The small word in the middle is doing the counting for you, and it agrees with the thing named in front of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read is or are as a count of the thing before it.

payload.prompt_text: You rent a flat and two things need repairing. Write two short sentences describing what the heating is like and what the windows are like.

feedback.why_key: Nothing is happening in either sentence. Both only report how things stand, which is exactly the job this word does.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the thing, then say what it is like.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 1 card about your home and where you eat. Speak for forty seconds. Each time you describe something rather than report an event, check afterwards whether you said is or are, and whether it matched what you had just named.

feedback.why_key: Under speed the choice is made by the nearest word rather than by the thing the sentence is about, and that is where it slips.
feedback.feed_forward: Pause on the thing you named before you choose is or are.

points.title: Never leaving the front of a sentence empty: I, you, he, she, it, we, they

point_json.grammar_name: Subject pronouns, and the rule that English never drops the subject

teach.can_do: I can keep the front of every sentence filled, even when the meaning would survive without it.
teach.why_it_matters: Whole languages leave this out and English never does. It is the most visible mark of a beginner, and it costs one short word to fix.
teach.meaning: English keeps a seat at the front of every sentence and it will not leave that seat empty. Once you have named a person or a thing, you swap the name for a short stand-in word — I, you, he, she, it, we, they — so you do not keep repeating it. What you may never do is take the name away and put nothing there instead. Even when nobody real is doing anything, as with weather and time, English still parks an it in the seat.

form.pattern: I · you · he · she · it · we · they — one of them in front of the action word, every time
notes: he for a man or a boy, she for a woman or a girl, it for a thing, an animal, the weather or the time.
they for more than one of anything, and for one person whose gender you do not know.
The stand-in word replaces the name. You do not say both, one after the other.
form.negative: The stand-in word stays in the seat when the sentence goes negative: it is not raining, they are not open.
form.question: Ask who or what is in the seat. If the honest answer is nobody, the sentence is not finished yet.

left.role: the seat English never leaves empty

right.text: is raining hard on the coast road

spec.caption: Nothing real is doing the raining. English fills the seat anyway, every single time.

worked_example.sentence: Ines drives the early bus, and she knows every passenger by name.
worked_example.why_this_form: Ines is named once. The second half swaps the name for she, so the sentence stops repeating it and the seat still has somebody sitting in it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Leave that second seat empty and the reader gets a half-sentence which seems to hand the knowing to the bus rather than to the driver.

notice_set.sentence: It is raining again on the coast road.
notice_set.question: Who or what is doing the raining?
notice_set.why: Nothing real is doing it. English puts a word in the seat because the seat is never allowed to stand empty.

notice_set.sentence: Ines drives the early bus. She starts at half past four.
notice_set.question: Who starts at half past four?
notice_set.why: She points straight back to the last person named, so the second sentence is still about Ines.

notice_set.sentence: The two porters unlocked the hall. They left the side door open.
notice_set.question: Who left the door open?
notice_set.why: They points back to the two porters, so the news carries on being about the same two people.

notice_set.sentence: It gets dark by four here in December.
notice_set.question: What is this sentence about?
notice_set.why: The word in the seat points at nothing you could touch. The news is about how early the dark comes.

notice_set.sentence: Rafi and I share the shift on Saturdays.
notice_set.question: How many people work that shift?
notice_set.why: Two people are sitting in the seat together, so the news covers both of them at once.

teach.rule_line: Every English sentence needs somebody or something in the front seat, even when nobody is there.
teach.false_rule: That you may drop the stand-in word when the person is obvious from the sentence before. It is obvious to you. English still insists on the word.

errors.wrong: Is raining hard in Sandmouth this morning.
errors.right: It is raining hard in Sandmouth this morning.
errors.why_it_happens: In Spanish, Italian, Turkish and Chinese the seat can stay empty and nobody misses it. The sentence feels finished because in the writer's first language it would be.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: It.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Spanish, Italian, Turkish, Chinese and Japanese.

errors.wrong: My sister she works at the Brackenfield clinic.
errors.right: My sister works at the Brackenfield clinic.
errors.why_it_happens: The name is said first and the stand-in word arrives afterwards out of habit, so the seat ends up with two people in it. Several languages do exactly this.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: she.

errors.wrong: Rafi and me take the same bus every morning.
errors.right: Rafi and I take the same bus every morning.
errors.why_it_happens: Me is the shape used everywhere else in a sentence, so it turns up in the front seat too. Fluent speakers do this as well, which keeps it sounding possible.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: me becomes I.

pays_in.note: Dropping this word is the fastest way to sound like a beginner.
pays_in.model: I work in a small office and it takes me twenty minutes to get there.

pays_in.note: An essay sentence with an empty front seat stops the reader dead.
pays_in.model: It is often argued that cheaper fares would take cars off the roads.

pays_in.note: These words are short and unstressed, and they carry who is being talked about.
pays_in.model: They said they would ring when it was ready to collect.

used_in.quote: Answers on this card run on I and it, and an empty front seat is audible in the first ten seconds.

payload.sentence: Ines drives the early bus. She knows every stop by heart.
payload.question: Who knows every stop?

feedback.why_key: She points back to the last person named, which is how the second sentence stays about the same driver.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the short word back to the last person named.

payload.sentence: It rains on the Verdon nearly every day in March.
payload.question: What is this sentence about?

feedback.why_key: The word in the front seat points at nothing you could touch. The news is about the weather.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept it as a placeholder when nothing real is acting.

items.decision_cue: Is difficult to reach the office by bus

payload.context: From a first draft of a letter about transport.
payload.sentence: Is difficult to reach the office by bus before nine.
reasons: the front seat of the sentence has been left empty
the office has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The meaning is perfectly clear, which is exactly why the gap survives redrafting. English still refuses to start here.
feedback.feed_forward: Start the sentence with It when nothing else can go there.

payload.context: From a paragraph about evening classes.
payload.stem: ___ is cheaper to study part time than to give up work.

expected: it

feedback.why_key: Nobody is doing the being cheaper, so English parks its placeholder in the seat and gets on with the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Fill an empty front seat with It before anything else.

payload.context: Talking about the people you live with.
payload.stem: My parents run a small shop, and ___ open it at seven.

expected: they

feedback.why_key: Two people were named a moment ago, so the second half swaps the name for the word that covers both of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap the name for a short word rather than repeating it.

payload.context: Build one sentence about the walk up from the station.

expected: it takes forty minutes to reach the depot on foot

feedback.why_key: Nothing is doing the taking. The placeholder goes first and the real news follows behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with It when the sentence has no real doer.

payload.given: Yusuf mends the machines. Yusuf trained at the Ashfield works.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that does not say the name twice.

expected: mends the machines and he trained at the ashfield works
mends the machines and trained at the ashfield works

feedback.why_key: The short word takes over the moment the name has done its job, and the reader still knows exactly who is meant.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the person once, then use the short word.

payload.audio_text: They're late again and it isn't even half past six.

expected: they're late again and it isn't even half past six
they are late again and it is not even half past six
theyre late again and it isnt even half past six

feedback.why_key: Both front-seat words are squeezed almost to nothing here, and losing them costs you who and what the speaker means.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the short word at the start of each half.

payload.sentence: My neighbour she complains about the noise from the depot every week.

expected: my neighbour complains
she complains

feedback.why_key: The seat has two people in it and only one of them is needed. Keep the name or keep the short word, never both.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete whichever of the two says the person twice.

items.decision_cue: Rafi and me share the late shift

payload.context: Answering a question about your working week.
payload.sentence: Rafi and me share the late shift on Thursdays.
reasons: the wrong shape of the word is sitting in the front seat
the shift has been put in the wrong place
the sentence needs a full stop in the middle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Take Rafi away and you would never say me share. The seat takes I, however many other people are sitting in it.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the other person and test the word on its own.

payload.context: Two lines from a report on the same estate.
sentences: It is quiet after the market closes.
They are quiet after the market closes.

points.title: Saying whether you mean one of something or more than one

teach.can_do: I can say whether I mean one of something or more than one, and spell it correctly.
teach.why_it_matters: The word for a thing changes shape when there is more than one, and every later rule about matching and about a and the is built on that change.
teach.meaning: A word that names a thing — a ticket, a river, a teacher — is a naming word. English marks the difference between one of them and more than one on the naming word itself, by adding s to the end. That mark is not decoration: it is how a reader knows whether to picture one thing or a crowd. A few very common naming words change in an older way instead, and some name things you cannot count at all, so they never take the mark however much of them there is.

form.pattern: one ticket → two tickets · one class → two classes · one city → two cities
notes: Add es after an s, sh, ch, x or z sound: buses, benches, boxes.
A naming word ending in a consonant plus y swaps the y for ies: city becomes cities, but day stays days.
Older changes, learned one at a time: man and men, woman and women, child and children, foot and feet, person and people.
Words for things you cannot count never take the mark: information, advice, equipment, research, furniture, luggage.
form.negative: Nothing changes when the sentence goes negative. The mark belongs to the naming word, not to the sentence.
form.question: Ask how many. If the answer is more than one, the naming word has to show it before anything else does.

teach.rule_line: Ask how many. More than one puts an s on the end of the naming word.

points.title: Using a and an the first time you mention one of something

point_json.grammar_name: The indefinite article: a and an

teach.can_do: I can put a or an in front of a thing I am mentioning for the first time.
teach.why_it_matters: English will not let a single countable thing stand bare. Leaving the small word out is quiet and constant, and a reader notices it in every sentence.
teach.meaning: When you name one thing and your listener has not met it yet, English puts a small word in front of it: a. Say I caught a bus and the listener knows there was one bus and that this is the first they have heard of it. The word becomes an when the next word begins with a vowel sound, purely so the two words do not collide in the mouth. It is used for one countable thing only, never for more than one and never for something you cannot count.

form.pattern: a + a naming word starting with a consonant sound · an + a naming word starting with a vowel sound
notes: The choice is made by sound and not by spelling: a university, a one-way street, an hour, an honest answer.
Only ever for one countable thing. Never with the more-than-one shape, and never with words like advice or luggage.
If a describing word comes first, the small word sits in front of that instead: a busy kitchen, an empty plate.
form.negative: The small word stays where it is when the sentence goes negative: there is not a bus until seven.
form.question: Ask two things: is it one of them, and is my listener meeting it for the first time? Two yeses means a or an.

left.text: a ticket · a hostel · a university

right.role: the next sound is a vowel

worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Drop both small words and the sentence still makes sense, but it now reads as scribbled notes, and that is exactly how a reader receives it.

points.title: Putting describing words in front of the thing, and never adding an s to them

teach.can_do: I can put a describing word in the right place and keep it the same shape however many things there are.
teach.why_it_matters: Two reds cars is a first-week slip that survives to a high level if nobody names it. It is cheap to fix now and expensive to leave alone.
teach.meaning: A describing word says what something is like: cold, empty, expensive. In English it goes in front of the thing it describes, and it never changes shape at all. It does not grow an s when there are three things instead of one, and it does not take a different ending for a man or a woman. Many languages do both of those, which is why both feel natural to write. The describing word can also come after is or are, and there too it stays exactly as it was.

form.pattern: describing word + naming word — a cold room, two cold rooms
notes: It comes first and never afterwards: never a room cold.
It never takes the mark for more than one: two cold rooms, and never two colds rooms.
It never changes for a man or a woman: a tall woman, a tall man, the same word both times.
After is or are it keeps the same shape: the rooms are cold.
form.negative: not goes with the word carrying the sentence rather than with the describing word: the room is not cold.
form.question: Ask what is it like. Put that word straight in front of the thing, and then leave it completely alone.

spec.caption: The left box never changes, however much the right box does.

worked_example.sentence: The two empty flats above the shop need new windows.
worked_example.why_this_form: Empty and new both sit in front of the things they describe, and neither of them grows an s even though flats and windows both did.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Write two emptys flats and a reader still understands you perfectly, which is the trap: the meaning arrives and the mistake stays put.

notice_set.question: How many rooms does she rent?
notice_set.why: The number is carried by the thing itself, so the word describing it has nothing to do and does not change.

notice_set.sentence: The old lifts in the north block are slow.
notice_set.question: What are the lifts like?
notice_set.why: One describing word comes in front of the lifts and the other comes after are, and both describe the same lifts.

notice_set.sentence: Gethin bought an expensive coat for the winter.
notice_set.question: How many coats did he buy?
notice_set.why: The counting is done by the small word at the front. Expensive says nothing at all about number.

notice_set.sentence: The tall man in the blue coat runs the stall.
notice_set.question: What is the man wearing?
notice_set.why: Two describing words, each in front of the thing it describes, and neither changed for the man.

notice_set.sentence: The rooms upstairs are cold in winter.
notice_set.question: What are those rooms like in winter?
notice_set.why: Here the describing word arrives after are instead of in front, and it still keeps exactly the same shape.

teach.rule_line: Describing words go in front of the thing and never change shape, however many things there are.
teach.false_rule: That a describing word has to match the thing it describes, the way it does in Spanish, French or Arabic. English describing words never move and never change.

errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on reds.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Spanish, French, Italian and Arabic.

points.title: Saying that something exists somewhere: there is and there are

teach.can_do: I can say that something exists somewhere, and match the small word to how many there are.
teach.why_it_matters: It is how English announces that something exists at all, and the word after there is decided by what comes next, which is the opposite of every other sentence.
teach.meaning: To announce that something exists somewhere, English does not begin with the thing. It begins with there, which points at nothing whatever, then puts is or are, and only then names the thing. There is a night bus. There are two night buses. Because the real thing arrives after the word that has to match it, you have to look forward rather than back, and this is the one place in the language where that happens.

form.pattern: There is + one thing · There are + more than one thing
notes: Choose is or are by looking forward at the thing that follows, never back at there.

points.title: Saying who something belongs to, with my, your, her and the added 's

teach.can_do: I can say who something belongs to, with a short word in front of it or with an added 's.
teach.why_it_matters: English marks ownership in front of the thing and never after it, and the word is chosen by the owner rather than by the thing owned.
teach.meaning: English has two ways of saying who something belongs to, and both of them go in front of the thing. The first is a short word: my, your, his, her, its, our, their. The second is an added 's on the owner: Nils's boots, the club's rules. Whichever you use, the choice is settled by the owner and never by the thing owned. His car and his keys are both his because he owns them; the car and the keys get no say in it.

form.pattern: my · your · his · her · its · our · their + the thing — or — the owner + 's + the thing
notes: Chosen by the owner: her brother, her brothers, her house, all her, because she is the owner.
Add 's to a person, an animal or a group: Nils's coach, the team's kit. Use of for a thing: the roof of the station.
its means belonging to it. it's means it is. Two different words that sound identical.
After the short word you never also use the: never the my coat.
form.negative: not belongs to the word carrying the sentence: that is not my bag.
form.question: Ask whose. The answer goes in front of the thing, as a short word or with an added 's.

points.title: Putting where and when in the order English expects

teach.can_do: I can put where and when at the end of a sentence in the order English expects.
teach.why_it_matters: English is rigid here and most languages are not. Getting it wrong never stops a reader understanding you, which is exactly why nobody corrects it and it lasts for years.
teach.meaning: Once a sentence has said who did what, it often adds where that happened and when. English puts those two in a fixed order: where first, then when. It also refuses to let either of them stand between the action word and the thing the action landed on. You may lift the when-part to the very front of the sentence instead, and English is perfectly happy with that. What it will not take is the two swapped over at the end, or either of them wedged into the middle.

form.pattern: who + does what + what to + where + when
notes: Where comes before when: she works at the depot on Saturdays.
Never between the action and the thing it lands on: not she books on Saturdays the late shift.
The when-part may move to the very front instead: on Saturdays she works at the depot.
How something is done, if you say it, comes before where: she works quietly at the depot on Saturdays.
form.negative: not stays beside the word carrying the sentence and changes nothing about this order.
form.question: Ask what, then where, then when, and write the answers down in that same order.

steps.gloss: the thing the action lands on

feedback.why_key: Both lines are ordinary English and report the same facts. What moves is which of the two the writer is building the paragraph around.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the time to the front to make it your topic.

payload.prompt_text: A friend is meeting you off a train in a town you both know. Write one sentence saying what you will do, where you will wait and when.

feedback.why_key: An arrangement fails on exactly these two pieces, so the sentence has to carry both of them and in the order a reader expects.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what, then where, then when, in one breath.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 2 card about a festival you took part in. Speak for forty seconds. Listen back and check that in every sentence the place came before the time, and that neither of them cut across the action.

feedback.why_key: A long spoken turn is mostly where and when, and at speed they arrive in the order you remembered them rather than the order English wants.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish the action before you add where or when.

points.title: Showing a reader where a sentence starts and where it stops

point_json.grammar_name: Sentence boundaries: the capital letter and the full stop

teach.can_do: I can show a reader exactly where each sentence starts and where it stops.
teach.why_it_matters: A reader who cannot see where one sentence ends has to read it twice. Nothing on the page is cheaper to fix or more expensive to leave.
teach.meaning: A written sentence carries two marks that tell a reader where it begins and where it stops: a capital letter at the start and a full stop at the end. Between those two marks sits one piece of news, built round one action word. Two pieces of news need two sets of marks. A comma is not strong enough to hold them apart, and no mark at all is worse still. If a group of words has no action word in it, it does not get its own pair of marks at all.

form.pattern: Capital letter + one piece of news, built round one action word + full stop
notes: A capital letter also starts a name: Marlow, Ines, Tuesday, March.
One full stop ends one sentence, and a comma cannot do that job on its own.
To hold two pieces of news inside one sentence, join them with and, but, or so.
A question ends with a question mark instead, and it still opens with a capital letter.
form.negative: not lives inside the sentence and changes nothing at all about the two marks.
form.question: Read from one capital letter to the next full stop. Is there exactly one action word, and does the stretch stand up on its own?

left.role: one piece of news, from capital to full stop

right.role: the next piece of news, with its own pair of marks

spec.caption: The full stop is a wall. A comma is a curtain, and it will not hold these apart.

worked_example.sentence: The paper printed the story on Monday. Nobody at the council replied.
worked_example.why_this_form: Two pieces of news, so two capital letters and two full stops. Each half stands up on its own and each has its own action word.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Join them with a comma alone and a reader takes the whole thing as one thought, then has to go back and pull it apart without help.

notice_set.sentence: The paper printed the story on Monday. Nobody at the council replied.
notice_set.question: How many separate pieces of news are here?
notice_set.why: Two full stops mark out two, and either half would still make sense standing on its own.

notice_set.sentence: The council met on Thursday, nobody mentioned the harbour road.
notice_set.question: Would a reader have to go back and read this again?
notice_set.why: The comma is too weak to hold two whole pieces of news apart, so they run together and the reader untangles them.

notice_set.sentence: The reporter waiting outside the town hall in the rain.
notice_set.question: Does this tell you a whole piece of news?
notice_set.why: It names somebody and describes them, and then it stops without ever saying what happened.

notice_set.sentence: Ines writes for the Marlow paper. She covers the harbour.
notice_set.question: How many people are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The second sentence opens a fresh pair of marks but carries on about the same person.

notice_set.sentence: Did the council answer the letter?
notice_set.question: Is the writer asking or telling?
notice_set.why: The mark at the end is a question mark, and the capital letter at the front does exactly the same job as always.

teach.rule_line: One capital, one piece of news with one action word, one full stop. Then start again.
teach.false_rule: That a comma is enough to hold two pieces of news apart when the sentence would otherwise be long. Length has nothing to do with it.

errors.wrong: The council met on Thursday nobody mentioned the harbour road.
errors.right: The council met on Thursday. Nobody mentioned the harbour road.
errors.why_it_happens: The two pieces of news are about the same meeting, so they arrive as one thought. The writing follows the thought instead of following the sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one full stop after Thursday.

errors.wrong: The paper printed the story, the council said nothing for a week.
errors.right: The paper printed the story. The council said nothing for a week.
errors.why_it_happens: The comma is standing in for the pause you would make out loud, which is exactly what it does in speech. On paper it cannot separate two whole pieces of news.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one comma into a full stop.

errors.wrong: The reporter waiting outside the town hall since early morning.
errors.right: The reporter waited outside the town hall since early morning.
errors.why_it_happens: The group of words is long and detailed, so it feels like a finished sentence. Nothing inside it ever says what happened.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: waiting becomes waited.

pays_in.note: The commonest punctuation error on the page, and the one that makes a reader stop.
pays_in.model: Fares rose again in March. Passenger numbers fell for the first time in years.

pays_in.note: A letter whose sentences run together reads as careless before it reads as anything.
pays_in.model: The lock was broken when I arrived. I reported it the same day.

pays_in.note: Sentence ends are how you find where one idea in a passage stops.
pays_in.model: The scheme was abandoned in its second year. Nothing replaced it.

used_in.quote: Answers on this prompt stack short claims one after another, which is where the boundaries between them start dissolving.

payload.sentence: The paper ran the story on Monday. The council replied on Friday.
payload.question: How many separate pieces of news are here?

feedback.why_key: Two full stops mark out two, and either half would stand up perfectly well on its own.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the full stops to count the pieces of news.

payload.sentence: Ines writes for the Marlow paper. She covers the harbour.
payload.question: How many people are being talked about?

feedback.why_key: A new pair of marks starts a new sentence, not a new person, and the short word points straight back at Ines.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a new sentence as new news, not a new person.

items.decision_cue: rang twice, nobody at the office

payload.context: From a first draft of a report about a local newspaper.
payload.sentence: The editor rang twice, nobody at the office picked up.
reasons: a comma has been asked to hold two whole pieces of news apart
the office has been put in the wrong place
the editor has been left out of the second half
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Out loud there is a pause here and a comma feels exactly right. On paper the two halves need a wall between them.
feedback.feed_forward: Test each half on its own before you use a comma.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a local newspaper.
payload.stem: The paper printed the story ___ the council said nothing.

expected: but
and
yet

feedback.why_key: A joining word is the other way of keeping two pieces of news in one sentence without asking a comma to do it alone.
feedback.feed_forward: Join two halves with a word, not with a comma.

payload.context: Talking about how you follow the news.
payload.stem: The reporter ___ (wait) outside the hall all morning.

expected: waited

feedback.why_key: One word turns a description of somebody into a piece of news, and only news is allowed its own pair of marks.
feedback.feed_forward: Give every stretch between two stops an action word.

payload.context: Build one sentence that holds two pieces of news together.

expected: the scheme ended in march and nothing replaced it

feedback.why_key: The joining word in the middle is what lets both pieces of news live between the same capital letter and the same full stop.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the joining word between the two halves.

payload.given: Fares rose again in March, passenger numbers fell for the first time.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it as one sentence held together by a joining word.

expected: rose again in march but passenger numbers fell for the first time
rose again in march and passenger numbers fell for the first time
rose again in march so passenger numbers fell for the first time

feedback.why_key: The comma alone could not hold the two halves apart. A joining word can, and it also says how the two are related.
feedback.feed_forward: Add a joining word where the comma was doing too much.

payload.audio_text: The story broke on Monday and the council replied on Friday.

expected: the story broke on monday and the council replied on friday

feedback.why_key: The joining word is a single unstressed sound, and it is the only thing holding the two halves in one sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small joining word between two halves.

payload.sentence: The scheme was abandoned in its second year, nothing replaced it.

expected: second year and nothing
second year but nothing
second year. nothing

feedback.why_key: Both halves are whole pieces of news, so the comma is being asked to do work that only a stop or a joining word can do.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace the comma with a stop or a joining word.

items.decision_cue: A photographer outside the town hall since eight

payload.context: From a draft news paragraph about a council meeting.
payload.sentence: A photographer outside the town hall since eight. The doors stayed shut.
reasons: the first stretch never says what happened
the town hall has been put in the wrong place
the two halves should have been joined with a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The second stretch is a proper piece of news and the first only sets a scene, so only one of them has earned its marks.
feedback.feed_forward: Check each stretch for a word saying what happened.

payload.context: Two lines from different drafts of the same report.
sentences: The council met and the harbour was discussed.
The council met. The harbour was discussed.
meanings: The two facts are offered as one connected piece of news.
The two facts are offered as two separate pieces of news.

feedback.why_key: Both are correct English and both report the same events. What changes is whether the reader is told to hold them together.
feedback.feed_forward: Join two halves when you want them read as one.

payload.prompt_text: Most people now meet the news through social media rather than a newspaper. Write two sentences about that, each with its own capital letter and its own full stop.

feedback.why_key: Two related claims are exactly where the comma creeps in, because they feel like one thought while you are writing them.
feedback.feed_forward: Stop the first claim fully before starting the second.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on news and social media. Read it from one full stop to the next and check that each stretch is one piece of news with one action word in it. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: In the last third of a timed answer the stops start disappearing, because there is no monitoring capacity left to place them.
feedback.feed_forward: Reread the final paragraph for missing stops first.
